title: Reading a Frame
objective: After this level you can analyze a single frame by looking at composition, setting, costume and where the actors stand.
summary: Mise-en-scène is everything put in front of the camera: setting, costume, lighting and where actors stand. Placement and size in the frame show who matters.

cards.headline: Pause any film. How much is one frame telling you?
cards.body: In Citizen Kane, a small boy plays in the snow, far back in the frame, while the adults indoors decide who will raise him. You haven't heard a word yet, and you already know who has the power. That's a frame talking.

cards.headline: Mise-en-scène: everything in front of the camera
cards.body: Critics call it mise-en-scène, French for "putting in the scene". It covers everything placed before the camera: the setting and its props, the costumes, the lighting, and the actors and where they stand. Yale's Film Analysis guide notes that the setting, which it calls décor, can amplify a character's emotion or a film's whole mood. Reading a frame means asking why each of those things is there.

cards.headline: Rooms and clothes do the talking
cards.body: Costume can signify character, advertise fashions, or make clear distinctions between characters: dress two rivals alike or apart, and you've said something before anyone speaks. Rooms speak too. Remember Level 17's Caligari? Its designers built sets with exaggerated dimensions and deformed angles to show a narrator's tortured mind. That's décor amplifying emotion at full volume.

cards.headline: Where people stand, and how big they look
cards.body: Shot scale can bring you close to a character or swallow them in their surroundings. Welles used it in Citizen Kane to show power shifting. The boy Kane is a small figure playing in the snow at the back of the shot while, indoors, adults arrange for someone else to raise him. Thanks to deep focus, both he and they stay sharp.

mascot.line: Keep this: size and distance in the frame are rarely neutral. Ask who is big, who is small and who is far away.

cards.headline: Reading a Frame: done
learned: Mise-en-scène: all that's put before the camera
Décor and costume carry mood and character
Size and distance in the frame show power
Deep focus lets near and far share a shot

questions.prompt: What does mise-en-scène cover when you read a frame?

options.label: Only the dialogue the actors speak
options.rationale: Mise-en-scène is what is placed before the camera, not the script.

options.label: Setting, costume, lighting and where the actors stand
Only the order in which the shots are cut
Only the music added after filming

questions.explanation: Mise-en-scène, "putting in the scene", covers setting, props, costume, lighting and the actors and their positions.

questions.prompt: A new film shows a boss large in the foreground and a nervous employee tiny in a far corner. What is the staging most likely telling you?

options.label: Nothing: placement in the frame is random
options.rationale: Shot scale and placement can show power, as in Citizen Kane.

options.label: That the employee is the film's villain
options.rationale: Being small and far away suggests weakness, not villainy.

options.label: That the scene was shot with a telephoto lens by mistake
options.rationale: The question is what the staging means, not a technical error.

options.label: That the boss holds the power in this relationship

questions.explanation: Like the boy lost in the snow in Citizen Kane, a small, distant figure is swallowed by the frame while the large one dominates.

questions.prompt: In Citizen Kane the boy far back in the snow and the adults up front are all sharp. Which Level 46 technique made that staging possible?

options.label: Deep focus, keeping near and far planes sharp at once
A canted angle tilting the frame
options.rationale: Tilting the frame doesn't change what is in focus.

options.label: Three-strip Technicolor
options.rationale: Citizen Kane is in black and white.

options.label: A sound bridge between scenes
options.rationale: That's a sound technique, not focus.

questions.explanation: Gregg Toland's deep focus kept faces and objects sharp in all parts of the screen, so near and far could share one frame.
